source_text: I mean, just as a thought exercise, imagine that I was working with your namesake Claude Shannon and we had to do the whole thing with punch cards.  We would be way more efficient than we are being.

fragments.text: I mean, just as a thought exercise, imagine that I was working with your namesake Claude Shannon and we had to do the whole thing with punch cards.
We would be way more efficient than we are being.

reply_text:
㊥ Yes, I agree. With punch cards, every run is expensive, so you'd read the source and work out what the run should print before submitting it. We've been doing the reverse: using 13-minute cold runs to find out things that reading the source would have told us. The clearest case tonight was `ks`. Three traced runs went in before I read `elaborate_own_declaration_header` and the import-linking code. Two minutes of reading gave the hypothesis that turned out right.

㊭ (what I'd change)
1. **Predict before running.** Every packet that ends in a cold run has to state the expected result first: the counts, the next stop, and which function handles the node. It works that out from the Lean source and the port source. If the run disagrees, that's a wrong hypothesis to understand from the source, not a reason to run again with another guess.
2. **I read first, at every stop.** When a run returns a new stop, I read the raise site and the code around it before sending anything. I send a hypothesis with file and line, not "trace it". When I did that tonight (`ks`, the `≥` term loss, the `fun _ => y` source), it went fast. When I sent "trace it" instead, it cost a run each time.
3. **Spend runs on confirmation, and batch them.** When fixes in different lanes are independent, one cold run on a combined branch checks all of them, instead of one run per fix per lane.
4. **Make the run itself cheap where possible.** That's the probe by source location (codex-30) and the cold-path measurement (codex-31). They help, but they're secondary. The main saving is in 1 and 2.

🈸 (do you want this as a rule?) I'd add 1 and 2 to the packet preamble and to my own review practice now, and apply 3 when merging. Shall I?

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: Yes. The probe asks Lean which module owns a constant name, and `Lean.__instance_4563` is the port's own synthetic name for an anonymous instance, so Lean has never heard of it. But the port's declaration record already holds its source file and line, `Init/Notation.lean:105`, and the module follows from the path. So the probe can take a source location instead of a name. I've sent that to codex-30, who was idle.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (codex-30, `invoke-1791238923646-33195`) The probe gets a second way in: a declaration by source path and line. It derives the owning module from the path (`Init/Notation.lean` → `Init.Notation`), then runs the same cold production compile of that one declaration with its dependencies. The compile path doesn't change. The check is to compile `Init/Notation.lean:105` this way, and compare its time with a full `mkListNode` cold run.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (side question in the packet) Lean gives that instance a generated `inst…` name, not `__instance_4563`. codex-30 will find Lean's actual name, and check whether the port's `__instance_N` names ever appear in a compared term. If they do, matching Lean's instance names becomes its own packet.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (why it matters) If compiling one declaration takes a minute or two instead of 14, every lane can reproduce its stop that way. Combined with the real-path rule, that removes most of the waiting.
